title: Multimodal Fusion via Self-Consistent Task-Gradient Fields
claim: Fusion designs distort the evidence distribution through missing inputs, objective conflicts and rigid alignment, degrading unimodal extractors, while ours stays robust.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right; Venn diagram, 3-row distribution grid, grouped bar charts
description: Three-panel teaser. Panel A, "What each modality contains", shows three tinted cards for Visual (blue), Audio (orange) and Text (pink), each with small icons. Below them is a large three-circle Venn diagram called "Evidence distribution". It marks modality-specific cues, weak shared cues in the overlaps, and a dashed purple decision-support region. Panel B, "How fusion disturbs the joint distribution", is a 3-row by 4-column grid. The rows are missing modality, objective conflict and rigid alignment. The columns run from disturbance source through unimodal distributions and disturbance mechanism to the disturbed joint distribution. Each cell holds 2-D Gaussian blobs with a dashed GT box, and arrows link the stages. Panel C, "Degradation caused by OOD", has three grouped bar charts, one per backbone pair, with negative accuracy and AUC drops for Cross-Attn, MI-Min and Contrastive. A green-outlined SCFAE column shows near-zero drops. The eye goes first to the Venn diagram, then to the tall red and yellow bars.
caption: Teaser of fusion-induced degradation. A: Modalities contain specific cues, shared cues, and decision-supporting evidence. B: Missing inputs, auxiliary-objective conflict, and rigid alignment disturb this evidence geometry. C: The resulting degradation weakens unimodal extractors, while SCFAE preserves task-gradient access and organized subspaces. Complete results are reported in Tab. [ref]
abstract: Multimodal learning aims to preserve as much task-related information as possible from different inputs. However, current fusion designs often distort the feedback loop to feature extractors. Aggressively merging modalities entangles their representations, making the feature extractors fragile to incomplete inputs. Meanwhile, attempting to separate features via auxiliary losses frequently introduces optimization conflicts that distract from the primary task. We propose the Self-Consistent Field Autoencoder (SCFAE) to provide a better path for task gradients. Our method follows the self-consistent field principle to balance task learning with feature organization, thereby minimizing mutual information. We use small autoencoders for each modality to keep information intact. The task loss acts as a driving force to select predictive features. The reconstruction loss acts as a constraint to separate these features into independent subspaces. These dual objectives operate through complementary feature subspaces, thereby mitigating optimization interference. We evaluate SCFAE on audio-visual-text, audio-visual, and image-video benchmarks. Results show that SCFAE handles missing data and unequal input sizes more robustly via a simple structure. Gradient analysis confirms that SCFAE avoids conflicts and maintains stable training dynamics.
